title: Chemistry — Pure and impure substances
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank, except where marked for KS3 Science (chemistry) (status of the source: authored-reviewed-reverified-2026-10-08). Terms and clues: C3#c12 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; C3#c16 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; C3#c17 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition; C3#c14 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition. assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Concentration
items.clue: How much of a substance there is in a given volume.

items.label: Distillation
items.clue: A method that gets the solvent back from a solution.

items.label: Paper chromatography
items.clue: Separates dissolved dyes as a solvent rises up a sheet.

items.label: Filtration
items.clue: A method that separates an insoluble solid from a liquid.

questions.stem: In science, what is a pure substance?

options.text: A natural material with nothing added to it
A material that looks clear and clean
Just one substance, with nothing mixed in
A single element, but not a compound

questions.explanation: Yes. A pure substance is a single element or a single compound with nothing else in it, such as distilled water or copper.

questions.stem: Sugar is added to water and dissolves. This makes a sugar solution. Which is the solute?

options.text: The water it dissolves in
The sugar solution as a whole
The sugar that dissolves
Nothing, as the sugar has gone

questions.explanation: Yes. The solute is the substance that dissolves, here the sugar. The water is the solvent, and the sugar solution is the mixture made.

questions.stem: A label says 'Pure spring water: natural, with nothing added'. Spring water has minerals dissolved in it. What is it to a scientist?

options.text: A mixture of water and minerals
A pure substance, as it is natural
A pure substance, as it looks so clear
A compound of water and minerals

questions.explanation: Yes. It contains water and dissolved minerals, which are not joined, so it is a mixture. To a scientist it is not pure.

questions.stem: Sugar is stirred into hot tea until it can no longer be seen. What has happened to the sugar?

options.text: It has melted and become liquid sugar
It has gone and is no longer in the tea
It reacted with water to make a new compound
Its particles have spread out in the water

questions.explanation: Yes. The sugar has dissolved: its particles have spread out among the water particles. The sugar is still there, which is why the tea tastes sweet.

questions.stem: Rock salt is dug from the ground. Salt is extracted from it by dissolving, filtering and evaporating. Which is purer, and why?

options.text: The rock salt, as it is natural and untouched
The rock salt, as extracting is a chemical change
Both are equally pure, as both are just salt
The extracted salt, as the rock and soil are removed

questions.explanation: Yes. Dissolving and filtering leave the insoluble rock and soil behind, so the extracted salt contains far fewer other substances. It is the same salt, just separated from the rest.

questions.stem: Salt is stirred into water until no more will dissolve. More salt is then added, at the same temperature. What happens to the extra salt, and why?

options.text: It stays solid, as salt is insoluble
It stays solid in the saturated solution
It dissolves if you stir for longer
It melts away into the salty water

questions.explanation: Yes. The solution is saturated: it holds as much salt as can dissolve at that temperature, so the extra salt stays as solid at the bottom.

questions.stem: To a scientist, which of these is a pure substance?

options.text: Clean mountain air
Fresh orange juice
Carbon dioxide gas
Filtered sea water

questions.explanation: A pure substance is a single element or compound; air, juice and sea water are all mixtures.

questions.stem: Chalk powder is stirred into water. The water turns cloudy, and later the chalk settles at the bottom. What does this show?

options.text: Chalk does not dissolve in water
Chalk has dissolved to make a solution
Chalk dissolves with more stirring
Chalk reacts to make a new substance

questions.explanation: Yes. Chalk is insoluble in water: its bits make the water cloudy and then settle out. A solution would be see-through, and nothing would settle out.

questions.stem: Salt is dissolved in water in a sealed flask. How does the mass of the solution compare with the mass of the salt and water before?

options.text: Less, as the salt has disappeared
Less, as dissolved salt weighs nothing
The same, as the salt is still there
More, as salty water is denser

questions.explanation: Yes. The salt particles are still there, spread out among the water particles, and the flask is sealed, so nothing escapes. Mass of solution = mass of salt + mass of water.
